questions.stem: Which property of carbon contributes most directly to the diversity of biological molecules?

options.text: It forms four covalent bonds and can produce chains, branches and rings
options.why: Four bonding positions let carbon connect to itself and other elements in many stable arrangements.

options.text: It forms only ionic bonds with hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen atoms
options.why: Carbon usually forms covalent bonds in biological molecules. Restricting it to ionic bonds would remove the bonding patterns the question asks about.

options.text: It can bond to four atoms but cannot form carbon–carbon double bonds
options.why: Carbon can form both single and double bonds. Those alternatives add to the range of structures it can produce.

options.text: It dissolves readily in water before cells assemble it into polymers
options.why: Solubility of elemental carbon doesn't explain molecular diversity. The important feature is the number and variety of covalent bonds carbon can form.

questions.stem: What happens during hydrolysis of a polysaccharide?

options.text: Water is added to break glycosidic bonds between sugar units
options.why: The water supplies H and OH to the products as a glycosidic bond is broken.

options.text: Water is released while glycosidic bonds form between sugar units
options.why: That describes condensation, which builds a larger carbohydrate instead of breaking one down.

options.text: Hydrogen is removed from every monosaccharide without changing any bonds
options.why: Hydrolysis changes a covalent bond and adds the components of water. It doesn't strip hydrogen from every monomer.

options.text: The polysaccharide dissolves in water but remains chemically unchanged
options.why: Dissolving is a physical process. Hydrolysis is a chemical reaction that breaks glycosidic bonds.

questions.stem: Why is glucose readily transported in aqueous fluids?

options.text: Its hydroxyl groups make it polar and able to interact with water
options.why: Glucose can form hydrogen bonds with water, so it dissolves and can travel in aqueous solutions.

options.text: Its hydrocarbon ring makes the whole molecule strongly non-polar
options.why: The several hydroxyl groups make glucose polar despite its carbon skeleton. A strongly non-polar molecule would be poorly soluble.

options.text: Its glycosidic bonds give each glucose molecule a full electrical charge
options.why: A free glucose molecule contains no glycosidic bond, and glucose remains neutral overall rather than carrying a full charge.

options.text: Its six carbon atoms allow it to separate into ions in water
options.why: Glucose dissolves as intact neutral molecules. Its carbon count doesn't cause ionization.

questions.stem: Which feature makes glycogen well suited to rapid mobilization of stored glucose?

options.text: Its many branches provide numerous ends for glucose removal
options.why: Enzymes can work at many branch ends, allowing glucose units to be mobilized from multiple sites.

options.text: Its beta-glucose units produce long straight chains for enzyme attachment
options.why: That resembles cellulose structure. Glycogen contains alpha-glucose and is highly branched.

options.text: Its phosphate groups make the polymer highly soluble in cytoplasm
options.why: Glycogen isn't built from phosphate-containing monomers. Its relative insolubility is useful for storage.

options.text: Its fatty-acid tails release individual glucose molecules by condensation
options.why: Glycogen has no fatty-acid tails. Glucose is removed from it by hydrolysis, not condensation.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly links cellulose structure to its function?

options.text: Alternating beta-glucose units form straight chains; neighboring chains hydrogen-bond into strong microfibrils
options.why: Straight chains align closely, and hydrogen bonding between them produces microfibrils with high tensile strength.

options.text: Alpha-glucose units form highly branched chains; branch points make the plant cell wall elastic
options.why: Alpha-glucose and branching describe storage polysaccharides. Cellulose contains beta-glucose and forms unbranched chains.

options.text: Beta-glucose units form coiled chains; ester bonds link the coils into waterproof fibers
options.why: Cellulose chains are straight rather than coiled, and neighboring chains associate through hydrogen bonds rather than ester bonds.

options.text: Alternating glucose units form separate monomers; ionic bonds attach them directly to the membrane
options.why: Cellulose is a covalently linked polymer in the cell wall. Glycosidic and hydrogen bonds, not ionic attachment to the membrane, explain its strength.

questions.stem: What allows a cell-surface glycoprotein to act in cell–cell recognition?

options.text: Its exposed carbohydrate chain has a specific recognizable shape
options.why: The arrangement of sugars creates a surface marker that other cells or immune molecules can recognize.

options.text: Its fatty-acid tails store enough energy to identify neighboring cells
options.why: Fatty-acid tails belong to lipids, not the recognition portion of a glycoprotein. Recognition depends on molecular shape.

options.text: Its glucose units enter neighboring cells and compare their DNA sequences
options.why: Cell recognition occurs through interactions at the cell surface. Carbohydrate chains don't enter cells to inspect DNA.

options.text: Its phosphate groups give every cell type the same surface charge
options.why: Identical surface charge wouldn't distinguish cell types. Specific carbohydrate structures provide the identifying differences.

questions.stem: Which products result from forming one triglyceride by condensation?

options.text: One triglyceride and three water molecules
options.why: Three ester bonds form between one glycerol and three fatty acids, releasing one water for each bond.

options.text: One phospholipid and one water molecule
options.why: A phospholipid contains phosphate and only two fatty-acid tails. Those aren't the components or water yield of triglyceride formation.

options.text: Three glycerol molecules and one fatty acid
options.why: The ratio is reversed. A triglyceride contains one glycerol joined to three fatty acids.

options.text: One polysaccharide and three carbon dioxide molecules
options.why: Polysaccharides form from monosaccharides. Carbon dioxide isn't released when ester bonds form in a triglyceride.

questions.stem: A fatty acid contains two C=C bonds. How should it be classified?

options.text: Polyunsaturated
options.why: Polyunsaturated fatty acids contain two or more carbon–carbon double bonds.

options.text: Saturated
options.why: A saturated fatty acid contains no C=C bonds and carries the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms.

options.text: Monounsaturated
options.why: A monounsaturated fatty acid contains exactly one C=C bond, not two.

options.text: Amphipathic
options.why: Amphipathic describes a molecule with hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions. It doesn't classify the number of C=C bonds.

questions.stem: Why do lipids rich in cis-unsaturated fatty acids generally have lower melting points?

options.text: Cis double bonds kink the chains and prevent close packing
options.why: Poorer packing weakens intermolecular attractions, so less energy is needed to separate the molecules.

options.text: Cis double bonds add full electrical charges that repel neighboring chains
options.why: Cis double bonds don't create full charges. Their main effect here is changing the chain's shape.

options.text: Cis double bonds remove every hydrogen atom from the fatty acid
options.why: Unsaturation removes fewer hydrogen atoms than that claim suggests. A fatty acid with a cis double bond still contains many hydrogens.

options.text: Cis double bonds create hydrogen bonds between adjacent hydrocarbon chains
options.why: Non-polar hydrocarbon chains don't form hydrogen bonds with one another. Kinks reduce their close contact.

questions.stem: Why are triglycerides effective long-term energy stores?

options.text: They are energy-dense and insoluble, so storage has little osmotic effect
options.why: Triglycerides release about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates and can be stored without drawing in large amounts of water.

options.text: They dissolve rapidly and produce a large osmotic gradient in storage cells
options.why: That would make storage disruptive. Triglycerides are hydrophobic and don't create a large osmotic effect.

options.text: They contain branched glucose chains with many sites for rapid hydrolysis
options.why: That describes glycogen. Triglycerides contain glycerol and fatty acids rather than glucose chains.

options.text: They form rigid microfibrils that resist stretching in adipose tissue
options.why: Rigid microfibrils are made from cellulose in plant walls. Adipose tissue stores triglyceride droplets.

questions.stem: How are phospholipids oriented in a bilayer surrounded by water?

options.text: Hydrophilic heads face water and hydrophobic tails face inward
options.why: This arrangement lets the polar heads interact with water while shielding the non-polar tails.

options.text: Hydrophobic heads face water and hydrophilic tails face inward
options.why: The properties have been reversed. The phosphate-containing heads are hydrophilic, while the hydrocarbon tails are hydrophobic.

options.text: Both heads and tails face water because the whole phospholipid is polar
options.why: A phospholipid is amphipathic rather than entirely polar. Its hydrocarbon tails avoid contact with water.

options.text: Both heads and tails face inward because the whole phospholipid is non-polar
options.why: The phosphate-containing heads are polar and interact with surrounding water, so they face outward.

questions.stem: Why can testosterone diffuse directly through a phospholipid bilayer?

options.text: It is largely non-polar and dissolves in the bilayer's hydrophobic core
options.why: Its lipid-soluble structure lets it enter the membrane interior and cross without a channel.

options.text: It carries a full charge that attracts the hydrophilic fatty-acid tails
options.why: Testosterone doesn't carry a full charge, and fatty-acid tails are hydrophobic rather than hydrophilic.

options.text: It is a polysaccharide that passes through carbohydrate transport proteins
options.why: Testosterone is a steroid lipid, not a polysaccharide. Its non-polarity allows direct diffusion.

options.text: It hydrolyzes membrane phospholipids and enters through the resulting gaps
options.why: Steroid diffusion doesn't require membrane damage. Testosterone dissolves in and crosses the intact bilayer.
